title: Reading together
hookLine: study groups, sutta circles, reading with a friend
tomorrow: one book fits in Mai's bag. who gets to choose it?

lines: THE BOOK CLUB NOBODY READS FOR.
GOOD FRIENDS: HALF THE HOLY LIFE.
cards: Somebody in the group chat says let's start a book club, and then nobody reads the book. Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, had a better time with company.
In the Samyutta Nikaya he comes to the Buddha with something warm to say: having good friends, good companions, is half of the holy life. A generous thing to say about friendship.
And the Buddha's answer begins, strangely: don't say that, Ananda. Why would the teacher push back on praise for friends?

teach.b: Because Ananda undersold it. The Buddha goes on: it isn't half.
Good friendship, kalyana-mittata, is the whole of the holy life. Someone with good friends can be expected to walk the whole path.

Then he makes it personal: people caught in birth, aging and death are set free by having him as their good friend. That's the puzzle solved. He isn't correcting Ananda for loving friendship too much.
Ananda didn't rate it high enough. And it's the teaching behind how Buddhists read.
Tradition says the first teachings were kept by monks reciting them together, out loud, before anyone wrote them down.

Now there are sutta circles in living rooms and on video calls: someone reads a passage aloud, the group sits in silence, then each person says what they heard. Notice what that adds to yesterday's single line.
Nobody has to be the expert; the reading is the teacher, and the silence is shared. Alone, you hear what you're ready to hear.

teach.h: EACH HEARS WHAT THE OTHER MISSED.
teach.b: Together, someone hears what you missed, and you catch what they missed.
In this sutta, a good friend on the path isn't a nice extra beside the practice. The friend is how the path gets walked.

how: Buddhist study groups, sometimes called sutta circles or dharma study groups, meet in homes, temples and online: a passage is read aloud, the group sits in silence, and then each person shares what they heard.

o: taking turns so the book gets finished sooner
sharing a text aloud with others and hearing them
quietly reading the same book in separate rooms

games.q: the puzzle and its answer — tap the pairs.
p: said friendship is half the path
said it's the whole of it
read aloud, sit, then each one speaks

s: in the sutta, the Buddha agrees that friendship is half the holy life
he says don't say that, Ananda: it isn't half, it's the whole.
reading a Buddhist text is meant to be a solo, silent practice
tradition says the teachings were first kept by reciting them together, and sutta circles still read aloud as a group.
the Buddha calls himself a good friend to the people he frees
in the same sutta, beings are set free by having him as their good friend.

games.q: your sutta circle reads a passage. one member jumps in to explain what it 'really means' before anyone else speaks. what fits today's teaching?
o: ask for a minute of silence, then let each person say what they heard
let the best-read person explain; that's what a good friend is for
skip the talking and just move on to the next passage
games.why: reading together works because each person hears what the others missed. the friend matters as a fellow listener, not only as an explainer.

practice: Choose one line you've read this year, from any text you love. Send it to one person you trust, just the line, nothing added. Then sit for two minutes with the same words, knowing someone else is holding them too.

wordCard.voice: Reading together: the same line held by two people, each hearing what the other missed.

orig.note: Pali: a good or admirable friend, one who walks the path with you. In this sutta the Buddha calls himself one.

carryVoice: Keep this one: together, because Ananda said half and the Buddha said the whole. Back tomorrow.

sources.ref: Cullavagga XI (the first recitation of the teachings)
